what_it_does: A technique called '3D Gaussian Splatting' represents a scene as millions of fuzzy, semi-transparent blobs (called Gaussians) and renders each video frame by computing every blob's color contribution at every pixel — a process called 'Gaussian blending.' On small edge devices like the NVIDIA Jetson used in AR/VR headsets, this blending step is the main bottleneck, achieving only 7-17 frames per second when immersive video requires at least 60. GBU (Gaussian Blending Unit) is a small add-on hardware block designed to be plugged into an existing edge GPU to accelerate only this blending stage. Its key trick is processing pixels left-to-right within each row: because neighboring pixels are close together, much of the coordinate math can be shared across them, cutting per-pixel work by up to 5.5x. It also detects early when a Gaussian contributes too little to a pixel (below a visibility threshold) and skips the rest of that Gaussian's calculation, reducing work by up to 93% in some cases. A small on-chip 'Gaussian Reuse Cache' keeps recently used blob parameters close by, cutting off-chip memory traffic by nearly half.
